15	NodeManager
16	===========
17	
18	<!-- MACRO{toc|fromDepth=0|toDepth=3} -->
19	
20	Overview
21	--------
22	
23	The NodeManager is responsible for launching and managing containers on a node. Containers execute tasks as specified by the AppMaster.
24	
25	
26	Health Checker Service
27	----------------------
28	
29	The NodeManager runs services to determine the health of the node it is executing on. The services perform checks on the disk as well as any user specified tests. If any health check fails, the NodeManager marks the node as unhealthy and communicates this to the ResourceManager, which then stops assigning containers to the node. Communication of the node status is done as part of the heartbeat between the NodeManager and the ResourceManager. The intervals at which the disk checker and health monitor(described below) run don't affect the heartbeat intervals. When the heartbeat takes place, the status of both checks is used to determine the health of the node.
30	
31	###Disk Checker
32	
33	  The disk checker checks the state of the disks that the NodeManager is configured to use(local-dirs and log-dirs, configured using yarn.nodemanager.local-dirs and yarn.nodemanager.log-dirs respectively). The checks include permissions and free disk space. It also checks that the filesystem isn't in a read-only state. The checks are run at 2 minute intervals by default but can be configured to run as often as the user desires. If a disk fails the check, the NodeManager stops using that particular disk but still reports the node status as healthy. However if a number of disks fail the check(the number can be configured, as explained below), then the node is reported as unhealthy to the ResourceManager and new containers will not be assigned to the node.
34	
35	The following configuration parameters can be used to modify the disk checks:
36	
37	| Configuration Name | Allowed Values | Description |
38	|:---- |:---- |:---- |
39	| `yarn.nodemanager.disk-health-checker.enable` | true, false | Enable or disable the disk health checker service |
40	| `yarn.nodemanager.disk-health-checker.interval-ms` | Positive integer | The interval, in milliseconds, at which the disk checker should run; the default value is 2 minutes |
41	| `yarn.nodemanager.disk-health-checker.min-healthy-disks` | Float between 0-1 | The minimum fraction of disks that must pass the check for the NodeManager to mark the node as healthy; the default is 0.25 |
42	| `yarn.nodemanager.disk-health-checker.max-disk-utilization-per-disk-percentage` | Float between 0-100 | The maximum percentage of disk space that may be utilized before a disk is marked as unhealthy by the disk checker service. This check is run for every disk used by the NodeManager. The default value is 90 i.e. 90% of the disk can be used. |
43	| `yarn.nodemanager.disk-health-checker.min-free-space-per-disk-mb` | Integer | The minimum amount of free space that must be available on the disk for the disk checker service to mark the disk as healthy. This check is run for every disk used by the NodeManager. The default value is 0 i.e. the entire disk can be used. |
44	
45	### External Health Script
46	
47	Users may specify their own health checker scripts that will be invoked by the health checker service. Users may specify a timeout as well as options to be passed to the script. If the script times out, results in an exception being thrown or outputs a line which begins with the string ERROR, the node is marked as unhealthy. Please note that:
48	
49	  * Exit code other than 0 is **not** considered to be a failure because it might have been caused by a syntax error. Therefore the node will **not** be marked as unhealthy.
50	
51	  * If the script cannot be executed due to permissions or an incorrect path, etc, then it counts as a failure and the node will be reported as unhealthy.
52	
53	  * Specifying a health check script is not mandatory. If no script is specified, only the disk checker status will be used to determine the health of the node.
54	
55	Users can specify up to 4 scripts to run individually with the `yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.scripts` configuration. Also these options can be configured for all scripts (global configurations):
56	
57	| Configuration Name | Allowed Values | Description |
58	|:---- |:---- |:---- |
59	|`yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.script`| String | The keywords for the health checker scripts separated by a comma. The default is "script". |
60	| `yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.interval-ms` | Positive integer | The interval, in milliseconds, at which health checker service runs; the default value is 10 minutes. |
61	| `yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.timeout-ms` | Positive integer | The timeout for the health script that's executed; the default value is 20 minutes. |
62	
63	The following options can be set for every health checker script. The %s symbol is substituted with each keyword provided in `yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.script`.
64	
65	| Configuration Name | Allowed Values | Description |
66	|:---- |:---- |:---- |
67	| `yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.%s.path` | String | Absolute path to the health check script to be run. Mandatory argument for each script. |
68	| `yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.%s.opts` | String | Arguments to be passed to the script when the script is executed. Mandatory argument for each script. |
69	| `yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.%s.interval-ms` | Positive integer | The interval, in milliseconds, at which health checker service runs.  |
70	| `yarn.nodemanager.health-checker.%s.timeout-ms` | Positive integer | The timeout for the health script that's executed. |
71	
72	The interval and timeout options are not required to be specified. In that case the global configurations will be used.
73	
74	NodeManager Restart
75	-------------------
76	
77	### Introduction
78	
79	This document gives an overview of NodeManager (NM) restart, a feature that enables the NodeManager to be restarted without losing the active containers running on the node. At a high level, the NM stores any necessary state to a local state-store as it processes container-management requests. When the NM restarts, it recovers by first loading state for various subsystems and then letting those subsystems perform recovery using the loaded state.
80	
81	### Enabling NM Restart
82	
83	Step 1. To enable NM Restart functionality, set the following property in **conf/yarn-site.xml** to *true*.
84	
85	| Property | Value |
86	|:---- |:---- |
87	| `yarn.nodemanager.recovery.enabled` | `true`, (default value is set to false) |
88	
89	Step 2.  Configure a path to the local file-system directory where the NodeManager can save its run state.
90	
91	| Property | Description |
92	|:---- |:---- |
93	| `yarn.nodemanager.recovery.dir` | The local filesystem directory in which the node manager will store state when recovery is enabled. The default value is set to `$hadoop.tmp.dir/yarn-nm-recovery`. |
94	
95	Step 3: Enable NM supervision under recovery to prevent running containers from getting cleaned up when NM exits.
96	
97	| Property | Description |
98	|:---- |:---- |
99	| `yarn.nodemanager.recovery.supervised` | If enabled, NodeManager running will not try to cleanup containers as it exits with the assumption it will be immediately be restarted and recover containers The default value is set to 'false'. |
100	
101	Step 4.  Configure a valid RPC address for the NodeManager.
102	
103	| Property | Description |
104	|:---- |:---- |
105	| `yarn.nodemanager.address` | Ephemeral ports (port 0, which is default) cannot be used for the NodeManager's RPC server specified via yarn.nodemanager.address as it can make NM use different ports before and after a restart. This will break any previously running clients that were communicating with the NM before restart. Explicitly setting yarn.nodemanager.address to an address with specific port number (for e.g 0.0.0.0:45454) is a precondition for enabling NM restart. |
106	
107	Step 5.  Auxiliary services.
108	
109	  * NodeManagers in a YARN cluster can be configured to run auxiliary services. For a completely functional NM restart, YARN relies on any auxiliary service configured to also support recovery. This usually includes (1) avoiding usage of ephemeral ports so that previously running clients (in this case, usually containers) are not disrupted after restart and (2) having the auxiliary service itself support recoverability by reloading any previous state when NodeManager restarts and reinitializes the auxiliary service.
110	
111	  * A simple example for the above is the auxiliary service 'ShuffleHandler' for MapReduce (MR). ShuffleHandler respects the above two requirements already, so users/admins don't have to do anything for it to support NM restart: (1) The configuration property **mapreduce.shuffle.port** controls which port the ShuffleHandler on a NodeManager host binds to, and it defaults to a non-ephemeral port. (2) The ShuffleHandler service also already supports recovery of previous state after NM restarts.
112	
113	  * There are two ways to configure auxiliary services, through a manifest or through the Configuration. Auxiliary services will only be loaded via the prior method of using Configuration properties when an auxiliary services manifest is not enabled. One advantage of using a manifest is that NMs can dynamically reload auxiliary services based on changes to the manifest. To support reloading, AuxiliaryService implementations must perform any cleanup that is needed during the service stop phase for the NM to be able to create a new instance of the auxiliary service.
114	
115	Auxiliary Service Classpath Isolation
116	-------------------------------------
117	
118	### Introduction
119	To launch auxiliary services on a NodeManager, users have to add their jar to NodeManager's classpath directly, thus put them on the system classloader. But if multiple versions of the plugin are present on the classpath, there is no control over which version actually gets loaded. Or if there are any conflicts between the dependencies introduced by the auxiliary services and the NodeManager itself, they can break the NodeManager, the auxiliary services, or both. To solve this issue, we can instantiate auxiliary services using a classloader that is different from the system classloader.
120	
121	### Manifest
122	This section describes the auxiliary service manifest for aux-service classpath isolation.
123	To use a manifest, the property `yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.manifest.enabled` must be set to true in *yarn-site.xml*.
124	
125	To load the manifest file from a filesystem, set the file path in *yarn-site.xml* under the property `yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.manifest`. The NMs will check this file for new modifications at an interval specified by `yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.manifest.reload-ms` (defaults to 0; setting interval <= 0 means it will not be reloaded automatically).
126	Alternatively, the manifest file may be sent to an NM via REST API by making a PUT call to the endpoint `http://nm-http-address:port/ws/v1/node/auxiliaryservices`. Note this only updates the manifest on one NM.
127	When it reads a new manifest, the NM will add, remove, or reload auxiliary services as needed based on the service names and versions found in the manifest.
128	
129	An example manifest that configures classpath isolation for a CustomAuxService follows. One or more files may be specified to make up the classpath of a service, with jar or archive formats being supported.
130	```
131	{
132	  "services": [
133	    {
134	      "name": "mapreduce_shuffle",
135	      "version": "2",
136	      "configuration": {
137	        "properties": {
138	          "class.name": "org.apache.hadoop.mapred.ShuffleHandler",
139	          "mapreduce.shuffle.transfer.buffer.size": "102400",
140	          "mapreduce.shuffle.port": "13562"
141	        }
142	      }
143	    },
144	    {
145	      "name": "CustomAuxService",
146	      "version": "1",
147	      "configuration": {
148	        "properties": {
149	          "class.name": "org.aux.CustomAuxService"
150	        },
151	        "files": [
152	          {
153	            "src_file": "${remote-dir}/CustomAuxService.jar",
154	            "type": "STATIC"
155	          },
156	          {
157	            "src_file": "${remote-dir}/CustomAuxService.tgz",
158	            "type": "ARCHIVE"
159	          }
160	        ]
161	      }
162	    }
163	  ]
164	}
165	```
166	
167	### Configuration
168	This section describes the configuration variables for aux-service classpath isolation. Aux services will only be loaded from the configuration if a manifest file is not specified.
169	
170	The following settings need to be set in *yarn-site.xml*.
171	
172	|Configuration Name | Description |
173	|:---- |:---- |
174	| `yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.%s.classpath` | Provide local directory which includes the related jar file as well as all the dependencies’ jar file. We could specify the single jar file or use ${local_dir_to_jar}/* to load all jars under the dep directory. |
175	| `yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.%s.remote-classpath` | Provide remote absolute or relative path to jar file(We also support zip, tar.gz, tgz, tar and gz files as well). For the same aux-service class, we can only specify one of the configurations: yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.%s.classpath or yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.%s.remote-classpath. The YarnRuntimeException will be thrown. Please also make sure that the owner of the jar file must be the same as the NodeManager user and the permbits should satisfy (permbits & 0022)==0 (such as 600, it's not writable by group or other).|
176	| `yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.%s.system-classes` | Normally, we do not need to set this configuration. The class would be loaded from customized classpath if it does not belongs to system-classes. For example, by default, the package org.apache.hadoop is in the system-classes, if your class CustomAuxService is in the package org.apache.hadoop, it would not be loaded from customized classpath. To solve this, either we could change the package for CustomAuxService, or configure our own system-classes which exclude org.apache.hadoop. |
177	
178	### Configuration Examples
179	
180		<property>
181			<name>yarn.nodemanager.aux-services</name>
182			<value>mapreduce_shuffle,CustomAuxService</value>
183		</property>
184	
185		<property>
186			<name>yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.CustomAuxService.classpath</name>
187			<value>${local_dir_to_jar}/CustomAuxService.jar</value>
188		</property>
189	
190	    <!--
191		<property>
192			<name>yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.CustomAuxService.remote-classpath</name>
193			<value>${remote-dir_to_jar}/CustomAuxService.jar</value>
194		</property>
195	    -->
196	
197		<property>
198			<name>yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.CustomAuxService.class</name>
199			<value>org.aux.CustomAuxService</value>
200		</property>
201	
202		<property>
203			<name>yarn.nodemanager.aux-services.mapreduce_shuffle.class</name>
204			<value>org.apache.hadoop.mapred.ShuffleHandler</value>
205		</property>
206	
207	Prevent Container Logs From Getting Too Big
208	-------------------------------------------
209	
210	This allows a cluster admin to configure a cluster such that a task attempt will be killed if any container log exceeds a configured size. This helps prevent logs from filling disks and also prevent the need to aggregate enormous logs.
211	
212	### Configuration
213	
214	The following parameters can be used to configure the container log dir sizes.
215	
216	| Configuration Name | Allowed Values | Description |
217	|:---- |:---- |:---- |
218	| `yarn.nodemanager.container-log-monitor.enable` | true, false | Flag to enable the container log monitor which enforces container log directory size limits. Default is false. |
219	| `yarn.nodemanager.container-log-monitor.interval-ms` | Positive integer | How often to check the usage of a container's log directories in milliseconds. Default is 60000 ms. |
220	| `yarn.nodemanager.container-log-monitor.dir-size-limit-bytes` | Long | The disk space limit, in bytes, for a single container log directory. Default is 1000000000. |
221	| `yarn.nodemanager.container-log-monitor.total-size-limit-bytes` | Long | The disk space limit, in bytes, for all of a container's logs. The default is 10000000000. |
222	
223	Scale Heart-beat Interval Based on CPU Utilization
224	-------------------------------------------------
225	
226	This allows a cluster admin to configure a cluster to allow the heart-beat between the Resource Manager and each NodeManager to be scaled based on the CPU utilization of the node compared to the overall CPU utilization of the cluster. 
227	
228	### Configuration
229	
230	The following parameters can be used to configure the heart-beat interval and whether and how it scales.
231	
232	| Configuration Name | Allowed Values | Description |
233	|:---- |:---- |:---- |
234	| `yarn.resourcemanager.nodemanagers.heartbeat-interval-ms` | Long | Specifies the default heart-beat interval in milliseconds for every NodeManager in the cluster. Default is 1000 ms. |
235	| `yarn.resourcemanager.nodemanagers.heartbeat-interval-scaling-enable` | true, false | Enables heart-beat interval scaling.  If true, The NodeManager heart-beat interval will scale based on the difference between the CPU utilization on the node and the cluster-wide average CPU utilization. Default is false. |
236	| `yarn.resourcemanager.nodemanagers.heartbeat-interval-min-ms` | Positive Long | If heart-beat interval scaling is enabled, this is the minimum heart-beat interval in milliseconds. Default is 1000 ms. |
237	| `yarn.resourcemanager.nodemanagers.heartbeat-interval-max-ms` | Positive Long | If heart-beat interval scaling is enabled, this is the maximum heart-beat interval in milliseconds. Default is 1000 ms. |
238	| `yarn.resourcemanager.nodemanagers.heartbeat-interval-speedup-factor` | Positive Float | If heart-beat interval scaling is enabled, this controls the degree of adjustment when speeding up heartbeat intervals. At 1.0, 20% less than the average cluster-wide CPU utilization will result in a 20% decrease in the heartbeat interval. Default is 1.0. |
239	| `yarn.resourcemanager.nodemanagers.heartbeat-interval-slowdown-factor` | Positive Float | If heart-beat interval scaling is enabled, this controls the degree of adjustment when slowing down heartbeat intervals. At 1.0, 20% greater than the average cluster-wide CPU utilization will result in a 20% increase in the heartbeat interval. Default is 1.0. |

NUMA Awareness
--------------

### Introduction

NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) is a computer memory design used in multiprocessing, where the memory access time depends on the memory location relative to the processor. Under NUMA, a processor can access its own local memory faster than non-local memory (memory local to another processor or memory shared between processors). The NodeManager can be made NUMA aware so that containers are launched with CPU and memory bound to specific NUMA nodes, which improves the performance of the applications.

### Prerequisites

  * NUMA awareness is supported only for the containers launched through the LinuxContainerExecutor.

  * The `numactl` command must be installed on each NodeManager node. It is used to read the NUMA topology of the node (with `numactl --hardware`) and to launch containers bound to the allocated NUMA nodes.

### Enabling NUMA Awareness

To enable NUMA awareness, set the following property to `true` in **conf/yarn-site.xml** on every NodeManager node:

| Property | Value |
|:---- |:---- |
| `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.enabled` | `true`, (default value is set to false) |

### Configuring the NUMA topology

The NodeManager can discover the NUMA topology of the node in two ways, controlled by the following configuration parameters:

| Configuration Name | Allowed Values | Description |
|:---- |:---- |:---- |
| `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.read-topology` | true, false | Whether to read the NUMA topology from the system using the command `numactl --hardware`. If the value is false then the NodeManager reads the topology from the configurations `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.node-ids` (for node id's), `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.<NODE_ID>.memory` (for each node memory) and `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.<NODE_ID>.cpus` (for each node cpus). Default value is false. |
| `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.node-ids` | Comma separated list of NUMA node ids | NUMA node id's in the form of a comma separated list. Memory and number of CPUs must be specified for each node using `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.<NODE_ID>.memory` and `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.<NODE_ID>.cpus` for each id specified in this value. This property value will be read only when `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.read-topology` is false. |
| `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.numactl.cmd` | String | The absolute path to the `numactl` command used to read the topology and to launch NUMA aware containers. Default value is `/usr/bin/numactl`. |

For example, if `yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.node-ids=0,1` then the memory (in MB) and the CPUs of the node id's `0` and `1` need to be specified like below:

```
yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.0.memory=73717
yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.0.cpus=6
yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.1.memory=73727
yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.1.cpus=6
```
EOF
echo done

args.new_string: 5.  HDFS supports non-volatile storage class memory (SCM, also known as persistent memory) cache in Linux platform. User can enable either memory cache or SCM cache for a DataNode. Memory cache and SCM cache can coexist among DataNodes. HDFS also supports SCM cache persistence. If `dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.recovery` is set to true, the DataNode will recover the persisted cache state on SCM during startup, and re-caching data is avoided. If this property is disabled, the DataNode will clean up the previous SCM cache, if any, and the data needs to be recached.

187:### Isolation
188:Router supports assignment of the dedicated number of RPC handlers to achieve isolation for all downstream nameservices it is configured to proxy. Since large or busy clusters may have relatively higher RPC traffic to the namenode compared to other clusters namenodes, this feature if enabled allows admins to configure higher number of RPC handlers for busy clusters. If dedicated handlers are not assigned for specific nameservices, equal distribution of RPC handlers is done for all configured nameservices. **Note** Fanout calls are treated as targeting a special nameservice, thus can be configured with handlers as well.
194:Overall the isolation feature is exposed via a configuration dfs.federation.router.handler.isolation.enable. The default value of this feature will be “false”. Users can also introduce their own fairness policy controller for custom allocation of handlers to various nameservices.
497:### Isolation
499:Isolation and dedicated assignment of RPC handlers across all configured downstream nameservices. The sum of these numbers must be strictly smaller than the total number of router handlers (configed by dfs.federation.router.handler.count).
503:| dfs.federation.router.fairness.policy.controller.class | `org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.federation.fairness.NoRouterRpcFairnessPolicyController` | Default handler allocation model to be used if isolation feature is enabled. Recommend to use `org.apache.hadoop.hdfs.server.federation.fairness.StaticRouterRpcFairnessPolicyController` to fully use the feature. |

185	        </property>
186	
187	*   **dfs.ha.fencing.methods** - a list of scripts or Java classes which will be used to fence the Active NameNode during a failover
188	
189	    It is critical for correctness of the system that only one NameNode be in the
190	    Active state at any given time. Thus, during a failover, we first ensure that
191	    the Active NameNode is either in the Standby state, or the process has
192	    terminated, before transitioning another NameNode to the Active state. In
193	    order to do this, you must configure at least one **fencing method.** These are
194	    configured as a carriage-return-separated list, which will be attempted in order
195	    until one indicates that fencing has succeeded. There are two methods which
196	    ship with Hadoop: *shell* and *sshfence*. For information on implementing
197	    your own custom fencing method, see the *org.apache.hadoop.ha.NodeFencer* class.
198	
199	    - - -
200	
201	    **sshfence** - SSH to the Active NameNode and kill the process
202	
203	    The *sshfence* option SSHes to the target node and uses *fuser* to kill
204	    the process listening on the service's TCP port. In order for this fencing option
205	    to work, it must be able to SSH to the target node without providing a
206	    passphrase. Thus, one must also configure the
207	    **dfs.ha.fencing.ssh.private-key-files** option, which is a
208	    comma-separated list of SSH private key files. For example:
209	
210	            <property>
211	              <name>dfs.ha.fencing.methods</name>
212	              <value>sshfence</value>
213	            </property>
214	    
215	            <property>
216	              <name>dfs.ha.fencing.ssh.private-key-files</name>
217	              <value>/home/exampleuser/.ssh/id_rsa</value>
218	            </property>
219	
220	    Optionally, one may configure a non-standard username or port to perform the
221	    SSH. One may also configure a timeout, in milliseconds, for the SSH, after
222	    which this fencing method will be considered to have failed. It may be
223	    configured like so:
224	
225	        <property>
226	          <name>dfs.ha.fencing.methods</name>
227	          <value>sshfence([[username][:port]])</value>
228	        </property>
229	        <property>
230	          <name>dfs.ha.fencing.ssh.connect-timeout</name>
231	          <value>30000</value>
232	        </property>
233	
234	    - - -
235	
236	    **shell** - run an arbitrary shell command to fence the Active NameNode
237	
238	    The *shell* fencing method runs an arbitrary shell command. It may be
239	    configured like so:
240	  
241	        <property>
242	          <name>dfs.ha.fencing.methods</name>
243	          <value>shell(/path/to/my/script.sh arg1 arg2 ...)</value>
244	        </property>
245	  
246	    The string between '(' and ')' is passed directly to a bash shell and may not
247	    include any closing parentheses.
248	  
249	    The shell command will be run with an environment set up to contain all of the
250	    current Hadoop configuration variables, with the '\_' character replacing any
251	    '.' characters in the configuration keys. The configuration used has already had
252	    any namenode-specific configurations promoted to their generic forms -- for example
253	    **dfs\_namenode\_rpc-address** will contain the RPC address of the target node, even
254	    though the configuration may specify that variable as
255	    **dfs.namenode.rpc-address.ns1.nn1**.
256	  
257	    Additionally, the following variables referring to the target node to be fenced
258	    are also available:
259	
260	    | | |
261	    |:---- |:---- |
262	    | $target\_host | hostname of the node to be fenced |
263	    | $target\_port | IPC port of the node to be fenced |
264	    | $target\_address | the above two, combined as host:port |
265	    | $target\_nameserviceid | the nameservice ID of the NN to be fenced |
266	    | $target\_namenodeid | the namenode ID of the NN to be fenced |
267	
268	    These environment variables may also be used as substitutions in the shell
269	    command itself. For example:
270	
271	        <property>
272	          <name>dfs.ha.fencing.methods</name>
273	          <value>shell(/path/to/my/script.sh --nameservice=$target_nameserviceid $target_host:$target_port)</value>
274	        </property>
275	
276	    If the shell command returns an exit
277	    code of 0, the fencing is determined to be successful. If it returns any other
278	    exit code, the fencing was not successful and the next fencing method in the
279	    list will be attempted.
280

1 14 15 #set ( $H3 = '###' ) 16 #set ( $H4 = '####' ) 17 18 DistCp Guide 19 ===================== 20 21 --- 22 23 - [Overview](#Overview) 24 - [Usage](#Usage) 25 - [Basic Usage](#Basic_Usage) 26 - [Update and Overwrite](#Update_and_Overwrite) 27 - [Sync](#Sync) 28 - [Command Line Options](#Command_Line_Options) 29 - [Architecture of DistCp](#Architecture_of_DistCp) 30 - [DistCp Driver](#DistCp_Driver) 31 - [Copy-listing Generator](#Copy-listing_Generator) 32 - [InputFormats and MapReduce Components](#InputFormats_and_MapReduce_Components) 33 - [Appendix](#Appendix) 34 - [Map sizing](#Map_sizing) 35 - [Copying Between Versions of HDFS](#Copying_Between_Versions_of_HDFS) 36 - [MapReduce and other side-effects](#MapReduce_and_other_side-effects) 37 - [Frequently Asked Questions](#Frequently_Asked_Questions) 38 39 --- 40 41 Overview 42 -------- 43 44 DistCp (distributed copy) is a tool used for large 45 inter/intra-cluster copying. It uses MapReduce to effect its distribution, 46 error handling and recovery, and reporting. It expands a list of files and 47 directories into input to map tasks, each of which will copy a partition of 48 the files specified in the source list. 49 50 [The erstwhile implementation of DistCp] 51 (http://hadoop.apache.org/docs/r1.2.1/distcp.html) has its share of quirks 52 and drawbacks, both in its usage, as well as its extensibility and 53 performance. The purpose of the DistCp refactor was to fix these 54 shortcomings, enabling it to be used and extended programmatically. New 55 paradigms have been introduced to improve runtime and setup performance, 56 while simultaneously retaining the legacy behaviour as default. 57 58 This document aims to describe the design of the new DistCp, its spanking new 59 features, their optimal use, and any deviance from the legacy implementation. 60 61 Usage 62 ----- 63 64 $H3 Basic Usage 65 66 The most common invocation of DistCp is an inter-cluster copy: 67 68 bash$ hadoop distcp hdfs://nn1:8020/foo/bar \ 69 hdfs://nn2:8020/bar/foo 70 71 This will expand the namespace under `/foo/bar` on nn1 into a temporary file, 72 partition its contents among a set of map tasks, and start a copy on each 73 NodeManager from `nn1` to `nn2`. 74 75 One can also specify multiple source directories on the command line: 76 77 bash$ hadoop distcp hdfs://nn1:8020/foo/a \ 78 hdfs://nn1:8020/foo/b \ 79 hdfs://nn2:8020/bar/foo 80 81 Or, equivalently, from a file using the -f option: 82 83 bash$ hadoop distcp -f hdfs://nn1:8020/srclist \ 84 hdfs://nn2:8020/bar/foo 85 86 Where `srclist` contains 87 88 hdfs://nn1:8020/foo/a 89 hdfs://nn1:8020/foo/b 90 91 When copying from multiple sources, DistCp will abort the copy with an error 92 message if two sources collide, but collisions at the destination are 93 resolved per the [options](#Command_Line_Options) specified. By default, 94 files already existing at the destination are skipped (i.e. not replaced by 95 the source file). A count of skipped files is reported at the end of each 96 job, but it may be inaccurate if a copier failed for some subset of its 97 files, but succeeded on a later attempt. 98 99 It is important that each NodeManager can reach and communicate with both the 100 source and destination file systems. For HDFS, both the source and 101 destination must be running the same version of the protocol or use a 102 backwards-compatible protocol; see [Copying Between Versions] 103 (#Copying_Between_Versions_of_HDFS). 104 105 After a copy, it is recommended that one generates and cross-checks a listing 106 of the source and destination to verify that the copy was truly successful. 107 Since DistCp employs both Map/Reduce and the FileSystem API, issues in or 108 between any of the three could adversely and silently affect the copy. Some 109 have had success running with `-update` enabled to perform a second pass, but 110 users should be acquainted with its semantics before attempting this. 111 112 It's also worth noting that if another client is still writing to a source 113 file, the copy will likely fail. Attempting to overwrite a file being written 114 at the destination should also fail on HDFS. If a source file is (re)moved 115 before it is copied, the copy will fail with a `FileNotFoundException`. 116 117 Please refer to the detailed Command Line Reference for information on all 118 the options available in DistCp. 119 120 $H3 Update and Overwrite 121 122 `-update` is used to copy files from source that don't exist at the target 123 or differ from the target version. `-overwrite` overwrites target-files that 124 exist at the target. 125 126 The Update and Overwrite options warrant special attention since their 127 handling of source-paths varies from the defaults in a very subtle manner. 128 Consider a copy from `/source/first/` and `/source/second/` to `/target/`, 129 where the source paths have the following contents: 130 131 hdfs://nn1:8020/source/first/1 132 hdfs://nn1:8020/source/first/2 133 hdfs://nn1:8020/source/second/10 134 hdfs://nn1:8020/source/second/20 135 136 When DistCp is invoked without `-update` or `-overwrite`, the DistCp defaults 137 would create directories `first/` and `second/`, under `/target`. Thus: 138 139 distcp hdfs://nn1:8020/source/first hdfs://nn1:8020/source/second hdfs://nn2:8020/target 140 141 would yield the following contents in `/target`: 142 143 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/first/1 144 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/first/2 145 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/second/10 146 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/second/20 147 148 When either `-update` or `-overwrite` is specified, the **contents** of the 149 source-directories are copied to target, and not the source directories 150 themselves. Thus: 151 152 distcp -update hdfs://nn1:8020/source/first hdfs://nn1:8020/source/second hdfs://nn2:8020/target 153 154 would yield the following contents in `/target`: 155 156 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/1 157 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/2 158 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/10 159 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/20 160 161 By extension, if both source folders contained a file with the same name 162 (say, `0`), then both sources would map an entry to `/target/0` at the 163 destination. Rather than to permit this conflict, DistCp will abort. 164 165 Now, consider the following copy operation: 166 167 distcp hdfs://nn1:8020/source/first hdfs://nn1:8020/source/second hdfs://nn2:8020/target 168 169 With sources/sizes: 170 171 hdfs://nn1:8020/source/first/1 32 172 hdfs://nn1:8020/source/first/2 32 173 hdfs://nn1:8020/source/second/10 64 174 hdfs://nn1:8020/source/second/20 32 175 176 And destination/sizes: 177 178 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/1 32 179 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/10 32 180 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/20 64 181 182 Will effect: 183 184 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/1 32 185 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/2 32 186 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/10 64 187 hdfs://nn2:8020/target/20 32 188 189 `1` is skipped because the file-length and contents match. `2` is copied 190 because it doesn't exist at the target. `10` and `20` are overwritten since 191 the contents don't match the source. 192 193 If `-update` is used, `1` is skipped because the file-length and contents match. `2` is copied because it doesn’t exist at the target. `10` and `20` are overwritten since the contents don’t match the source. However, if `-append` is additionally used, then only `10` is overwritten (source length less than destination) and `20` is appended with the change in file (if the files match up to the destination's original length). 194 195 If `-overwrite` is used, `1` is overwritten as well. 196 197 $H3 Sync 198 199 `-diff` option syncs files from a source cluster to a target cluster with a 200 snapshot diff. It copies, renames and removes files in the snapshot diff list. 201 202 `-update` option must be included when `-diff` option is in use. 203 204 Most cloud providers don't work well with sync at the moment. 205 206 Usage: 207 208 hadoop distcp -update -diff 209 210 Example: 211 212 hadoop distcp -update -diff snap1 snap2 /src/ /dst/ 213 214 The command above applies changes from snapshot `snap1` to `snap2` 215 (i.e. snapshot diff from `snap1` to `snap2`) in `/src/` to `/dst/`. 216 Obviously, it requires `/src/` to have both snapshots `snap1` and `snap2`. 217 But the destination `/dst/` must also have a snapshot with the same 218 name as ``, in this case `snap1`. The destination `/dst/` 219 should not have new file operations (create, rename, delete) since `snap1`. 220 Note that when this command finishes, a new snapshot `snap2` will NOT be 221 created at `/dst/`. 222 223 `-update` is required to use `-diff` option. 224 225 For instance, in `/src/`, if `1.txt` is added and `2.txt` is deleted after 226 the creation of `snap1` and before creation of `snap2`, the command above 227 will copy `1.txt` from `/src/` to `/dst/` and delete `2.txt` from `/dst/`. 228 229 Sync behavior will be elaborated using experiments below. 230 231 $H4 Experiment 1: Syncing diff of two adjacent snapshots 232 233 Some preparations before we start. 234 235 # Create source and destination directories 236 hdfs dfs -mkdir /src/ /dst/ 237 # Allow snapshot on source 238 hdfs dfsadmin -allowSnapshot /src/ 239 # Create a snapshot (empty one) 240 hdfs dfs -createSnapshot /src/ snap1 241 # Allow snapshot on destination 242 hdfs dfsadmin -allowSnapshot /dst/ 243 # Create a from_snapshot with the same name 244 hdfs dfs -createSnapshot /dst/ snap1 245 246 # Put one text file under /src/ 247 echo "This is the 1st text file." > 1.txt 248 hdfs dfs -put 1.txt /src/ 249 # Create the second snapshot 250 hdfs dfs -createSnapshot /src/ snap2 251 252 # Put another text file under /src/ 253 echo "This is the 2nd text file." > 2.txt 254 hdfs dfs -put 2.txt /src/ 255 # Create the third snapshot 256 hdfs dfs -createSnapshot /src/ snap3 257 258 Then we run distcp sync: 259 260 hadoop distcp -update -diff snap1 snap2 /src/ /dst/ 261 262 The command above should succeed. `1.txt` will be copied from `/src/` to 263 `/dst/`. 376	  * Input-formats and Map-Reduce components
377	
378	$H3 DistCp Driver
379	
380	  The DistCp Driver components are responsible for:
381	
382	  * Parsing the arguments passed to the DistCp command on the command-line,
383	    via:
384	
385	     * OptionsParser, and
386	     * DistCpOptionsSwitch
387	
388	  * Assembling the command arguments into an appropriate DistCpOptions object,
389	    and initializing DistCp. These arguments include:
390	
391	     * Source-paths
392	     * Target location
393	     * Copy options (e.g. whether to update-copy, overwrite, which
394	       file-attributes to preserve, etc.)
395	
396	  * Orchestrating the copy operation by:
397	
398	     * Invoking the copy-listing-generator to create the list of files to be
399	       copied.
400	     * Setting up and launching the Hadoop Map-Reduce Job to carry out the
401	       copy.
402	     * Based on the options, either returning a handle to the Hadoop MR Job
403	       immediately, or waiting till completion.
404	
405	  The parser-elements are exercised only from the command-line (or if
406	  DistCp::run() is invoked). The DistCp class may also be used
407	  programmatically, by constructing the DistCpOptions object, and initializing
408	  a DistCp object appropriately.
409	
410	$H3 Copy-listing Generator
411	
412	  The copy-listing-generator classes are responsible for creating the list of
413	  files/directories to be copied from source. They examine the contents of the
414	  source-paths (files/directories, including wild-cards), and record all paths
415	  that need copy into a SequenceFile, for consumption by the DistCp Hadoop
416	  Job. The main classes in this module include:
417	
418	  1. `CopyListing`: The interface that should be implemented by any
419	     copy-listing-generator implementation. Also provides the factory method by
420	     which the concrete CopyListing implementation is chosen.
421	  2. `SimpleCopyListing`: An implementation of `CopyListing` that accepts multiple
422	     source paths (files/directories), and recursively lists all the individual
423	     files and directories under each, for copy.
424	  3. `GlobbedCopyListing`: Another implementation of `CopyListing` that expands
425	     wild-cards in the source paths.
426	  4. `FileBasedCopyListing`: An implementation of `CopyListing` that reads the
427	     source-path list from a specified file.
428	
429	  Based on whether a source-file-list is specified in the DistCpOptions, the
430	  source-listing is generated in one of the following ways:
431	
432	  1. If there's no source-file-list, the `GlobbedCopyListing` is used. All
433	     wild-cards are expanded, and all the expansions are forwarded to the
434	     SimpleCopyListing, which in turn constructs the listing (via recursive
435	     descent of each path).
436	  2. If a source-file-list is specified, the `FileBasedCopyListing` is used.
437	     Source-paths are read from the specified file, and then forwarded to the
438	     `GlobbedCopyListing`. The listing is then constructed as described above.
439	
440	  One may customize the method by which the copy-listing is constructed by
441	  providing a custom implementation of the CopyListing interface. The behaviour
442	  of DistCp differs here from the legacy DistCp, in how paths are considered
443	  for copy.
444	
445	  One may also customize the filtering of files which shouldn't be copied
446	  by passing the current supported implementation of CopyFilter interface
447	  or a new implementation can be written. This can be specified by setting the
448	  `distcp.filters.class` in the DistCpOptions:
449	
450	  1. `distcp.filters.class` to "RegexCopyFilter". If you are using this implementation,
451	     you will have to pass along "CopyFilter" `distcp.filters.file` which contains the
452	     regex used for filtering. Support regular expressions specified by
453	     java.util.regex.Pattern.
454	  2. `distcp.filters.class` to "RegexpInConfigurationFilter". If you are using this
455	     implementation, you will have to pass along the regex also using
456	     `distcp.exclude-file-regex` parameter in "DistCpOptions". Support regular
457	     expressions specified by java.util.regex.Pattern. This is a more dynamic approach
458	     as compared to "RegexCopyFilter".
459	  3. `distcp.filters.class` to "TrueCopyFilter". This is used as a default
460	     implementation if none of the above options are specified.
461	
462	  The legacy implementation only lists those paths that must definitely be
463	  copied on to target. E.g. if a file already exists at the target (and
464	  `-overwrite` isn't specified), the file isn't even considered in the
465	  MapReduce Copy Job. Determining this during setup (i.e. before the MapReduce
466	  Job) involves file-size and checksum-comparisons that are potentially
467	  time-consuming.
468	
469	  The new DistCp postpones such checks until the MapReduce Job, thus reducing
470	  setup time. Performance is enhanced further since these checks are
471	  parallelized across multiple maps.
472	
473	$H3 InputFormats and MapReduce Components
474	
475	  The InputFormats and MapReduce components are responsible for the actual copy
476	  of files and directories from the source to the destination path. The
477	  listing-file created during copy-listing generation is consumed at this
478	  point, when the copy is carried out. The classes of interest here include:
479	
480	  * **UniformSizeInputFormat:**
481	    This implementation of org.apache.hadoop.mapreduce.InputFormat provides
482	    equivalence with Legacy DistCp in balancing load across maps. The aim of
483	    the UniformSizeInputFormat is to make each map copy roughly the same number
484	    of bytes. Apropos, the listing file is split into groups of paths, such
485	    that the sum of file-sizes in each InputSplit is nearly equal to every
486	    other map. The splitting isn't always perfect, but its trivial
487	    implementation keeps the setup-time low.
488	
489	  * **DynamicInputFormat and DynamicRecordReader:**
490	    The DynamicInputFormat implements `org.apache.hadoop.mapreduce.InputFormat`,
491	    and is new to DistCp. The listing-file is split into several "chunk-files",
492	    the exact number of chunk-files being a multiple of the number of maps
493	    requested for in the Hadoop Job. Each map task is "assigned" one of the
494	    chunk-files (by renaming the chunk to the task's id), before the Job is
495	    launched.
496	    Paths are read from each chunk using the `DynamicRecordReader`, and
497	    processed in the CopyMapper. After all the paths in a chunk are processed,
498	    the current chunk is deleted and a new chunk is acquired. The process
499	    continues until no more chunks are available.
500	    This "dynamic" approach allows faster map-tasks to consume more paths than
501	    slower ones, thus speeding up the DistCp job overall.
502	
503	  * **CopyMapper:**
504	    This class implements the physical file-copy. The input-paths are checked
505	    against the input-options (specified in the Job's Configuration), to
506	    determine whether a file needs copy. A file will be copied only if at least
507	    one of the following is true:
508	
509	     * A file with the same name doesn't exist at target.
510	     * A file with the same name exists at target, but has a different file
511	       size.
512	     * A file with the same name exists at target, but has a different
513	       checksum, and `-skipcrccheck` isn't mentioned.
514	     * A file with the same name exists at target, but `-overwrite` is
515	       specified.
516	     * A file with the same name exists at target, but differs in block-size
517	       (and block-size needs to be preserved.
518	
519	  * **CopyCommitter:** This class is responsible for the commit-phase of the
520	    DistCp job, including:
521	
522	     * Preservation of directory-permissions (if specified in the options)
523	     * Clean-up of temporary-files, work-directories, etc.
524	
525	Appendix
526	--------
527	
528	$H3 Map sizing
529	
530	  By default, DistCp makes an attempt to size each map comparably so that each
531	  copies roughly the same number of bytes. Note that files are the finest level
532	  of granularity, so increasing the number of simultaneous copiers (i.e. maps)
533	  may not always increase the number of simultaneous copies nor the overall
534	  throughput.
535	
536	  The new DistCp also provides a strategy to "dynamically" size maps, allowing
537	  faster data-nodes to copy more bytes than slower nodes. Using `-strategy
538	  dynamic` (explained in the Architecture), rather than to assign a fixed set
539	  of source-files to each map-task, files are instead split into several sets.
540	  The number of sets exceeds the number of maps, usually by a factor of 2-3.
541	  Each map picks up and copies all files listed in a chunk. When a chunk is
542	  exhausted, a new chunk is acquired and processed, until no more chunks
543	  remain.
544	
545	  By not assigning a source-path to a fixed map, faster map-tasks (i.e.
546	  data-nodes) are able to consume more chunks, and thus copy more data, than
547	  slower nodes. While this distribution isn't uniform, it is fair with regard
548	  to each mapper's capacity.
549	
550	  The dynamic-strategy is implemented by the `DynamicInputFormat`. It provides
551	  superior performance under most conditions.
552	
553	  Tuning the number of maps to the size of the source and destination clusters,
554	  the size of the copy, and the available bandwidth is recommended for
555	  long-running and regularly run jobs.
556	
557	$H3 Copying Between Versions of HDFS
558	
559	  For copying between two different major versions of Hadoop (e.g. between 1.X
560	  and 2.X), one will usually use WebHdfsFileSystem. Unlike the previous
561	  HftpFileSystem, as webhdfs is available for both read and write operations,
562	  DistCp can be run on both source and destination cluster.
563	  Remote cluster is specified as `webhdfs://<namenode_hostname>:<http_port>`.
564	  When copying between same major versions of Hadoop cluster (e.g. between 2.X
565	  and 2.X), use hdfs protocol for better performance.
566	
567	$H3 Secure Copy over the wire with distcp
568	  Use the "`swebhdfs://`" scheme when webhdfs is secured with SSL. For more information see [SSL Configurations for SWebHDFS](../hadoop-project-dist/hadoop-hdfs/WebHDFS.html#SSL_Configurations_for_SWebHDFS).
569	
570	$H3 MapReduce and other side-effects
571	
572	  As has been mentioned in the preceding, should a map fail to copy one of its
573	  inputs, there will be several side-effects.
574	
575	  * Unless `-overwrite` is specified, files successfully copied by a previous
576	    map on a re-execution will be marked as "skipped".
577	  * If a map fails `mapreduce.map.maxattempts` times, the remaining map tasks
578	    will be killed (unless `-i` is set).
579	  * If `mapreduce.map.speculative` is set set final and true, the result of the
580	    copy is undefined.
581	
582	$H3 DistCp and Object Stores
583	
584	DistCp works with Object Stores such as Amazon S3, Azure WASB and OpenStack Swift.
585	
586	Prequisites
587	
588	1. The JAR containing the object store implementation is on the classpath,
589	along with all of its dependencies.
590	1. Unless the JAR automatically registers its bundled filesystem clients,
591	the configuration may need to be modified to state the class which
592	implements the filesystem schema. All of the ASF's own object store clients
593	are self-registering.
594	1. The relevant object store access credentials must be available in the cluster
595	configuration, or be otherwise available in all cluster hosts.
596	
597	DistCp can be used to upload data
598	
599	```bash
600	hadoop distcp -direct hdfs://nn1:8020/datasets/set1 s3a://bucket/datasets/set1
601	```
602	
603	To download data
604	
605	```bash
606	hadoop distcp s3a://bucket/generated/results hdfs://nn1:8020/results
607	```
608	
609	To copy data between object stores
610	
611	```bash
612	hadoop distcp s3a://bucket/generated/results \
613	  wasb://updates@example.blob.core.windows.net
614	```
615	
616	And do copy data within an object store
617	
618	```bash
619	hadoop distcp wasb://updates@example.blob.core.windows.net/current \
620	  wasb://updates@example.blob.core.windows.net/old
621	```
622	
623	And to use `-update` to only copy changed files.
624	
625	```bash
626	hadoop distcp -update -numListstatusThreads 20  \
627	  swift://history.cluster1/2016 \
628	  hdfs://nn1:8020/history/2016
629	```
630	
631	Because object stores are slow to list files, consider setting the `-numListstatusThreads` option when performing a `-update` operation
632	on a large directory tree (the limit is 40 threads).
633	
634	When `DistCp -update` is used with object stores,
635	generally only the modification time and length of the individual files are compared,
636	not any checksums. The fact that most object stores do have valid timestamps
637	for directories is irrelevant; only the file timestamps are compared.
638	However, it is important to have the clock of the client computers close
639	to that of the infrastructure, so that timestamps are consistent between
640	the client/HDFS cluster and that of the object store. Otherwise, changed files may be
641	missed/copied too often.
642	
643	**Notes**
644	
645	* The `-atomic` option causes a rename of the temporary data, so significantly
646	increases the time to commit work at the end of the operation. Furthermore,
647	as Object Stores other than (optionally) `wasb://` do not offer atomic renames of directories
648	the `-atomic` operation doesn't actually deliver what is promised. *Avoid*.
649	
650	* The `-append` option is not supported.
651	
652	* The `-diff` and `rdiff` options are not supported
653	
654	* CRC checking will not be performed, irrespective of the value of the `-skipCrc`
655	flag.
656	
657	* All `-p` options, including those to preserve permissions, user and group information, attributes
658	checksums and replication are generally ignored. The `wasb://` connector will
659	preserve the information, but not enforce the permissions.
660	
661	* Some object store connectors offer an option for in-memory buffering of
662	output —for example the S3A connector. Using such option while copying
663	large files may trigger some form of out of memory event,
664	be it a heap overflow or a YARN container termination.
665	This is particularly common if the network bandwidth
666	between the cluster and the object store is limited (such as when working
667	with remote object stores). It is best to disable/avoid such options and
668	rely on disk buffering.
669	
670	* Copy operations within a single object store still take place in the Hadoop cluster
671	—even when the object store implements a more efficient COPY operation internally
672	
673	    That is, an operation such as
674	
675	      hadoop distcp s3a://bucket/datasets/set1 s3a://bucket/datasets/set2
676	
677	    Copies each byte down to the Hadoop worker nodes and back to the
678	bucket. As well as being slow, it means that charges may be incurred.
679	
680	* The `-direct` option can be used to write to object store target paths directly,
681	avoiding the potentially very expensive temporary file rename operations that would
682	otherwise occur.
683	
684	Frequently Asked Questions
685	--------------------------
686	
687	  1. **Why does -update not create the parent source-directory under a pre-existing target directory?**
688	     The behaviour of `-update` and `-overwrite` is described in detail in the
689	     Usage section of this document. In short, if either option is used with a
690	     pre-existing destination directory, the **contents** of each source
691	     directory is copied over, rather than the source-directory itself. This
692	     behaviour is consistent with the legacy DistCp implementation as well.
693	
694	  2. **How does the new DistCp differ in semantics from the Legacy DistCp?**
695	
696	     * Files that are skipped during copy used to also have their
697	       file-attributes (permissions, owner/group info, etc.) unchanged, when
698	       copied with Legacy DistCp. These are now updated, even if the file-copy
699	       is skipped.
700	     * Empty root directories among the source-path inputs were not created at
701	       the target, in Legacy DistCp. These are now created.
702	
703	  3. **Why does the new DistCp use more maps than legacy DistCp?**
704	     Legacy DistCp works by figuring out what files need to be actually copied
705	     to target before the copy-job is launched, and then launching as many maps
706	     as required for copy. So if a majority of the files need to be skipped
707	     (because they already exist, for example), fewer maps will be needed. As a
708	     consequence, the time spent in setup (i.e. before the M/R job) is higher.
709	     The new DistCp calculates only the contents of the source-paths. It
710	     doesn't try to filter out what files can be skipped. That decision is put
711	     off till the M/R job runs. This is much faster (vis-a-vis execution-time),
712	     but the number of maps launched will be as specified in the `-m` option,
713	     or 20 (default) if unspecified.
714	
715	  4. **Why does DistCp not run faster when more maps are specified?**
716	     At present, the smallest unit of work for DistCp is a file. i.e., a file
717	     is processed by only one map. Increasing the number of maps to a value
718	     exceeding the number of files would yield no performance benefit. The
719	     number of maps launched would equal the number of files.
720	
721	  5. **Why does DistCp run out of memory?**
722	     If the number of individual files/directories being copied from the source
723	     path(s) is extremely large (e.g. 1,000,000 paths), DistCp might run out of
724	     memory while determining the list of paths for copy. This is not unique to
725	     the new DistCp implementation.
726	     To get around this, consider changing the `-Xmx` JVM heap-size parameters,
727	     as follows:
728	
729	         bash$ export HADOOP_CLIENT_OPTS="-Xms64m -Xmx1024m"

    "CommandLine" attribute of the "java.exe" process to be fenced, for

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Filter a unified diff (git diff) keeping only hunks whose +/- lines match
any of the given regex patterns. Usage: filter_hunks.py <diff> <pat1> [pat2...]"""
import sys
import re

def main():
    path = sys.argv[1]
    rx = re.compile('|'.join('(?:%s)' % p for p in sys.argv[2:]))
    with open(path) as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
    out = []
    i, n = 0, len(lines)
    while i < n:
        if not lines[i].startswith('diff --git'):
            i += 1
            continue
        header = []
        while i < n and not lines[i].startswith('@@'):
            header.append(lines[i])
            i += 1
        kept = []
        while i < n and lines[i].startswith('@@'):
            hunk = []
            while i < n and not lines[i].startswith('@@') and \
                    not lines[i].startswith('diff --git'):
                hunk.append(lines[i])
                i += 1
            body = [l for l in hunk[1:]
                    if l[:1] in ('+', '-') and not l.startswith('+++')
                    and not l.startswith('---')]
            if any(rx.search(l) for l in body):
                kept.extend(hunk)
        if kept:
            out.extend(header)
            out.extend(kept)
    sys.stdout.write(''.join(out))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

5.  HDFS supports non-volatile storage class memory (SCM, also known as persistent memory) cache in Linux platform. User can enable either DRAM cache or SCM cache for a DataNode. DRAM cache and SCM cache can coexist among DataNodes. In addition, cache persistence is supported by SCM cache. The status of cache persisted in SCM will be recovered
during the start of DataNode if `dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.recovery` is set to true. Otherwise, previously persisted cache will be dropped and data need to be re-cached.
args.old_string: 5.  HDFS supports non-volatile storage class memory (SCM, also known as persistent memory) cache in Linux platform. User can enable either memory cache or SCM cache for a DataNode. Memory cache and SCM cache can coexist among DataNodes. HDFS also supports SCM cache persistence. If `dfs.datanode.pmem.cache.recovery` is set to true, the DataNode will recover the persisted cache state on SCM during startup, and re-caching data is avoided. If this property is disabled, the DataNode will clean up the previous SCM cache, if any, and the data needs to be recached.

new Access Point ARN. So, for example `s3a://sample-bucket/key` will now use your
configured ARN when getting data from S3 instead of your bucket.

You can also use an Access Point name as a path URI such as `s3a://finance-team-access/key`, by
configuring the `.accesspoint.arn` property as a per-bucket override:
```xml
<property>
    <name>fs.s3a.bucket.finance-team-access.accesspoint.arn</name>
    <value> {ACCESSPOINT_ARN_HERE} </value>
    <description>Configure S3a traffic to use this AccessPoint</description>
</property>
```

payload.resultSummary:
All 8 slugs in the hdfs-datanode-a batch are implemented and committed. Per-slug status:

- **async-disk-service-threadgroup (HDFS-16586): committed** (`5e34bf7232`) — removed the `threadGroup` field, its construction, and `new Thread(threadGroup, r)` → `new Thread(r)` in `FsDatasetAsyncDiskService.java`, so async-disk workers no longer drag BPServiceActor/DataNode threads into a custom thread group.
- **datanode-async-disk-workers (HDFS-16386): committed** (`7a5f888bcb`) — added `DFS_DATANODE_FSDATASETASYNCDISK_MAX_THREADS_PER_VOLUME_KEY/_DEFAULT` (=4) to `DFSConfigKeys.java`, a matching `hdfs-default.xml` property, and made `FsDatasetAsyncDiskService` read the config (rejecting non-positive values with `IllegalArgumentException`) instead of the hard-coded `MAXIMUM_THREADS_PER_VOLUME`.
- **datanode-log-placeholder (HDFS-16712): committed** (`4c97fc9f7a`) — `DataNode.getDiskBalancerStatus()` now logs `LOG.debug("Reading diskbalancer Status failed.", ex)` so the exception is attached as a throwable; empty-string return behavior unchanged.
- **datanode-metric-rate-error (HDFS-16311): committed** (`e7a8ce3409`) — `DataNodeVolumeMetrics.addFileIoError` now increments `fileIoErrorRate` instead of `metadataOperationRate`.
- **datanode-start-time-web (HDFS-16337): committed** (`60b8c7ae2c`) — added `getDNStartedTimeInMillis()` to `DataNodeMXBean` + `DataNode` (with `dnStartedTimeInMillis` field) and a `Started:` row (`{DNStartedTimeInMillis|date_tostring}`) in `webapps/datanode/datanode.html`.
- **datanode-start-time-rpc (HDFS-16350): committed** (`b4dd96fbce`) — removed the field initializer and set `dnStartedTimeInMillis = Time.now()` only after `ipcServer.start()` in `runDatanodeDaemon()`. Note: I deliberately committed this *after* start-time-web (the batch listed rpc first) because rpc modifies the field introduced by web; this also matches upstream order (HDFS-16337 → HDFS-16350).
- **datanode-simulated-config-removal (HDFS-16294): committed** (`6197d02581`) — the `CONFIG_PROPERTY_SIMULATED` constant itself was already absent from this tree; the only genuine remaining delta was the stale javadoc reference to it in `DataNode.startDataNode`, which I removed. No behavior or supported config keys changed.
- **bpserviceactor-register-namenode-log (HDFS-16627): committed** (`a43141cbdf`) — in `BPServiceActor.register()`, the handshake-begin, RemoteException, and successful-registration log messages now include the NameNode address (`nnAddr`); connection-problem messages already carried the address.

Verification: all 8 commits confirmed in `git log`, all 8 `requirement_patches/*.diff` files non-empty, each commit contains only the files I edited for that requirement (plus its own diff file). No Maven build was run (per instructions); changes were verified by careful code reading — imports were checked (`DFSConfigKeys` import added to `FsDatasetAsyncDiskService`, `Time` already available via `org.apache.hadoop.util.*` in `DataNode`), and `datanode.html` uses the existing `date_tostring` dust filter. Interleaved commits from other agents were left untouched; the shared TodoList was being overwritten by other agents so I tracked progress outside it.

# NUMA

Non-uniform memory access (NUMA) is a computer memory design used in multiprocessing,
where the memory access time depends on the memory location relative to the processor.
Under NUMA, a processor can access its own local memory faster than non-local memory
(memory local to another processor or memory shared between processors).
Yarn Containers can make benefit of this NUMA design to get better performance by binding to a
specific NUMA node and all subsequent memory allocations will be served by the same node,
reducing remote memory accesses. NUMA support for YARN Container has to be enabled only if worker
node machines has NUMA support.

# Enabling NUMA

### Prerequisites

- As of now, NUMA awareness works only with `LinuxContainerExecutor` (LCE)
- To use the feature of NUMA awareness in the cluster,It must be enabled with
  LinuxContainerExecutor (LCE)
- Steps to enable SecureContainer (LCE) for cluster is documented [here](SecureContainer.md)

## Configurations

**1) Enable/Disable the NUMA awareness**

This property enables the NUMA awareness feature in the Node Manager
for the containers. By default, the value of this property is false which means it is disabled.
If this property is `true` then only the below configurations will be applicable otherwise they
will be ignored.

In `yarn-site.xml` add

```
  <property>
     <name>yarn.nodemanager.numa-awareness.enabled</name>
     <value>true</value>
  </property>
```

**2) NUMA topology**

This property decides whether to read the NUMA topology from the system or from the
configurations. If this property value is true then the topology will be read from the system using
`numactl --hardware` command in UNIX systems and similar way in windows.
If this property is false then the topology will be read using the below configurations.
Default value of this configuration is false which means NodeManager will read the NUMA topology
from the below configurations.

+### Public datasets used in tests
+Some tests rely on the presence of existing public datasets available on Amazon S3.
+You may find a number of these in `org.apache.hadoop.fs.s3a.test.PublicDatasetTestUtils`.
+When testing against an endpoint which is not part of Amazon S3's standard commercial partition
+(`aws`) such as third-party implementations or AWS's China regions, you should replace these
+configurations with an empty space (` `) to disable the tests or an existing path in your object
+store that supports these tests.
+An example of this might be the MarkerTools tests which require a bucket with a large number of
+objects or the requester pays tests that require requester pays to be enabled for the bucket.
+It is always interesting when doing this to enable IOStatistics reporting
+```xml
+<property>
+  <name>fs.iostatistics.logging.level</name>
+  <value>info</value>
+</property>
+```
+# ---------------------------------------------------
+# Copy to from local
+# ---------------------------------------------------
+time bin/hadoop fs -copyFromLocal -t 10  share/hadoop/tools/lib/*aws*jar $BUCKET/
+# expect the iostatistics object_list_request value to be O(directories)
+bin/hadoop fs -ls -R $BUCKET/
+# expect the iostatistics object_list_request and op_get_content_summary values to be 1
+bin/hadoop fs -du -h -s $BUCKET/
+mkdir tmp
+time bin/hadoop fs -copyToLocal -t 10  $BUCKET/\*aws\* tmp
+# ---------------------------------------------------
+# Cloudstore
+# check out and build https://github.com/steveloughran/cloudstore
+# then for these tests, set CLOUDSTORE env var to point to the JAR
+# ---------------------------------------------------
+bin/hadoop jar $CLOUDSTORE storediag $BUCKET
+time bin/hadoop jar $CLOUDSTORE bandwidth 64M $BUCKET/testfile

import sys

def remove_block(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
    # find the banned-illegal-imports execution id
    idx = [i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if '<id>banned-illegal-imports</id>' in l]
    if len(idx) != 1:
        print(f"SKIP {path}: found {len(idx)} occurrences")
        return False
    i = idx[0]
    # search backwards for the enclosing <plugin> at some indentation
    start = None
    for j in range(i, -1, -1):
        s = lines[j].strip()
        if s == '<plugin>':
            start = j
            break
        if s == '</plugin>':
            print(f"SKIP {path}: hit </plugin> before <plugin>")
            return False
    if start is None:
        print(f"SKIP {path}: no <plugin> start")
        return False
    indent = lines[start][:len(lines[start]) - len(lines[start].lstrip())]
    # search forward for matching closing </plugin> at same indentation
    end = None
    for j in range(i, len(lines)):
        if lines[j] == indent + '</plugin>\n':
            end = j
            break
    if end is None:
        print(f"SKIP {path}: no closing </plugin>")
        return False
    # sanity: block must mention maven-enforcer-plugin and restrict-imports
    block = ''.join(lines[start:end+1])
    assert 'maven-enforcer-plugin' in block and 'restrictImports' in block, path
    del lines[start:end+1]
    with open(path, 'w') as f:
        f.writelines(lines)
    print(f"OK {path}: removed lines {start+1}-{end+1}")
    return True

for p in sys.argv[1:]:
    remove_block(p)
